rules.title: California security deposit cap and return rules (AB 12)
rules.requirement: Since July 1, 2024, a landlord may charge no more than one month's rent as a security deposit; small landlords may charge two months. Deposits must be returned within 21 days with an itemized statement, and landlords must offer a move-out walk-through inspection.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent; 2 months for small landlords
rules.coverage_conditions: All California residential tenancies. Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total, held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC of natural persons, may charge two months' rent.
rules.exemptions: Landlords owning only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total (natural person, family trust, or LLC with all natural-person members) may charge up to two months' rent.

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Rental housing providers may not inquire about, require disclosure of, or use criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection or decisions, and may not refuse to rent, terminate a tenancy, or charge more based on criminal history.
rules.coverage_conditions: All rental housing providers in Berkeley, except lifetime sex offenders, limited public housing/Section 8 exemptions, owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units, owner move-back units, and units where existing tenants sublet or add/replace roommates.
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; public housing/Section 8 properties (limited exemptions); owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back under BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units where existing tenants sublet or add/replace roommates.
rules.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation; civil damages including actual damages or three times one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

rules.title: Berkeley coordinated pricing algorithm ban
rules.requirement: No one may sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords, and no landlord may use, a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords and to persons who sell, license or provide coordinated pricing algorithms, for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.exemptions: Products that publish aggregated, anonymous rental data without recommending rents; products for setting rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines; and uses for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development.
rules.penalty: Civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each dwelling unit is a separate violation; prevailing party recovers attorney's fees and costs.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act annual rent cap (Civ. Code § 1947.12)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not raise the gross rent over any 12-month period by more than 5% plus the change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, above the lowest rent charged in the previous 12 months, and no more than twice in 12 months.
rules.key_value: 5% + CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential rental property, including units in mobilehome parks, subject to the listed exemptions; caps increases over any 12-month period and allows at most two increases in 12 months.
rules.exemptions: Affordable deed-restricted housing; dormitories; housing under stricter local rent control; housing certified for occupancy within 15 years (not mobilehomes); separately alienable condos/homes owned by non-corporate owners with notice; owner-occupied two-unit properties; mobilehome owners.
rules.penalty: Owner liable for injunctive relief, damages equal to the excess rent charged, and discretionary attorney's fees, plus up to treble damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct; the Attorney General or local city attorney may enforce; three-year limitations period.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act just cause eviction (Civ. Code § 1946.2)
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied residential real property for 12 months, the owner must not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written notice; for no-fault just cause the owner must give one month's rent relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent.
rules.key_value: 12 months' occupancy; 1 month's rent relocation or rent waiver
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property occupied 12 months or more, except housing certified for occupancy within 15 years, single-family owner-occupied homes with no more than two units or bedrooms, owner-occupied two-unit properties, separately alienable property held by non-corporate owners, and deed-restricted affordable housing.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly and adult residential facilities; school dormitories; housing certified for occupancy within 15 years; single-family owner-occupied residences and mobilehomes; owner-occupied two-unit structures; separately alienable property of non-corporate owners; deed-restricted affordable housing.
rules.penalty: Failure to comply renders the termination notice void; an owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary attorney's fees, and up to three times actual damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct.
rules.interaction: Yields to local just cause ordinances adopted on or before September 1, 2019, and to more protective local ordinances adopted or amended after that date; property is not subject to both.

rules.title: California security deposit limit (Civ. Code § 1950.5)

rules.title: FEHA criminal history and source-of-income screening protections
rules.requirement: Landlords may not consider arrests without conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile records, and may not blanket-ban applicants with criminal history. Conviction-based denial must be directly related to tenancy, and source-of-income discrimination, including refusing Section 8 vouchers, is barred.
rules.coverage_conditions: Most housing accommodations in California and most housing providers, including landlords, tenant screening companies, apartment managers, and property management companies.
rules.penalty: Remedies include out-of-pocket losses, injunctions, access to housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney’s fees.
rules.interaction: FEHA invalidates any state law to the extent it purports to require or permit unlawful housing discrimination.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: A rental property owner may not receive or use a coordinator's algorithmic revenue management service, and no person may perform a coordinating function or engage in parallel pricing coordination, including facilitating agreements among landlords that restrict competition on residential rents.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental property owners and coordinators of residential dwelling units in New Jersey; covers any house, apartment or accessory unit used as a primary residence, but not inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, or detention or correctional facilities.
rules.exemptions: Coordinating function excludes research/statistical analysis, free public rent estimates, equal-terms brokerage databases, and government affordability controls; government entities are not coordinators; conduct already unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act is unaffected.
rules.penalty: A violation is unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and sections 6 through 17 of P.L.1970, c.73 apply to a violation of section 4.
rules.interaction: Municipalities may not enact ordinances conflicting with the act; the act supplements rather than limits the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
